items.title: Cosell’s DOCTOR script, earlier state, Samson DECtape M46, 1966
items.creator: Cosell, Bernie (after Weizenbaum)
items.description:
The script for the Lisp ELIZA at I-2N9J5, read from GROSS ELI in slot 15 of DECtape M46 (tape identifier P14) in Peter Samson's collection. Byte-identical to the copy in Lars Brinkhoff's its-vault repository, which is where it was read from.

124 DEFPROP forms: 46 PRIORITY numbers, 47 RULES lists, 17 TRANSLATION entries for the contractions, 6 BELIEF flags and the single MEMR memory rule. The Lisp property list carries what Weizenbaum's script list structure carries.

It is the script printed in the appendix to the January 1966 CACM article, re-encoded. 65 keywords, every one of them present in the appendix, in the appendix's order, with nothing added. Keyword-sequence similarity against the transcription at P-J415Q is 0.94, the shortfall being MEMORY, NONE and XFREMD: the first two are handled in the program, and Weizenbaum's XFREMD is gone, the foreign-language reply hanging on DEUTSCH instead with FRANCAIS, ITALIANO and ESPANOL pointing at it.

The printed appendix carries the misprint PLEASE DON'T APOLIGIZE, and this file reads APOLOGIZE, as does Cosell's script tape of 2 July 1966 (I-9G8JQ).

The file carries DECtape read damage: TRANSLATIML for TRANSLATION, and OVERJ MY where a line break belongs. It ends in 0xFC block padding. It bears no date and no name.

items.name: Samson-1966-PDP6-ELIZA-gross.doc10.txt
items.title: Cosell’s DOCTOR adapted for PDP-6 Lisp, Samson DECtape M46, 1966
items.creator: Cosell, Bernie; PDP-6 adaptation unattributed (DECtape from Peter Samson’s collection)
items.description:
ELIZA in Lisp, from DECtape M46 (tape identifier P14) in Peter Samson's collection. Byte-identical to the copy in Lars Brinkhoff's its-vault repository, which is where it was read from. The repository's name is not the provenance: ITS did not exist when the tape was written.

The tape holds the working set in consecutive directory slots. GROSS DOC10 in slot 16 is this program: WORKER, READIN, ANALYZE, RECONSTRUCT and the TEST family, in Lisp property-list form. GROSS ELI in slot 15 is its script. GRUEN SCRIP4 in slot 17 is a further developed script whose first line reads "(QUOTE (UPDATED TO 16 JUN 66))". The extensions run against Weizenbaum's usage, since the .eli file holds the script and the .doc10 file the program.

Dating. The DECtape directory records name, extension and block count only, so no file here is dated from outside its own contents, and this one carries no date. What the tape supports is a working period. GROSS ELI reproduces the script printed in the appendix to the January 1966 CACM article: 65 keywords, every one present in the appendix, in the appendix's order, nothing added. GRUEN SCRIP4 departs from it, adding SVENSKA to the foreign-language reply and rules for monosyllabic answers, "bites the bag" and "my oh my", and carries the June 1966 date. Samson's own PDP-6 syntax-directed compiler, on the same tape, is dated 27 February, 9 March and 12 March 1965, and five of the twenty-three slots are empty, so the tape was written across at least sixteen months with deletions. The 1966 date therefore applies to the ELIZA group on the tape rather than to this file.

Source. The program was written from the published article and not from Weizenbaum's MAD-SLIP source, and it diverges from the source in three directions at once.

A feature the source carries and the article omits is absent here. At line 270 of the MAD-SLIP transcription Weizenbaum treats the word BUT as a delimiter beside the full stop and the comma, W'R WORD .E. $.$ .OR. WORD .E. $,$ .OR. WORD .E. $BUT$, whereas the article's statement of the rule says only that the program "recognizes a comma or a period as a delimiter". The article's own sample conversation can be reproduced only if BUT is a delimiter too, as Ciston et al. (2026, Inventing ELIZA, Table 1.1) and the annotated transcription of the source both note, so the delimiter was there to be inferred from the article; no version derived from it is known to have done so before Anthony Hay added BUT to his reimplementation after the source was found. This program has no word-level delimiter at all: a loop puts BREAK and PUNCTUATION on each of . , ( ) ! ? : ; and nothing else, and BUT occurs in the tape files only inside reply texts.

Features the article describes and the source lacks are present here. The annotated transcription of the source records that the recovered code does not support NEWKEY and does not order the keystack by precedence as the article describes. This program does both, NEWKEY popping the keystack in ANALYZE and SETKEYSTACK performing the article's priority insertion.

A parameter the article withholds is guessed. The article describes a counting mechanism deciding between a content-free reply and a stored memory without giving its period; the source runs LIMIT from 1 to 4 and delivers a memory at 4; this program uses a two-state toggle, (SETQ FLIPFLOP (PLUS 2 (MINUS FLIPFLOP))) against an initial 0, so a memory falls every other turn. The guess is Cosell's: his 1966 program at I-HJHZT sets the same FLIPFLOP.

A qualification: the recovered MAD-SLIP source is the 1965 state of Weizenbaum's program, and the article, written months later, describes NEWKEY and the ordered keystack, which a later state of his own code may have had. NEWKEY and the keystack therefore separate the article from the 1965 code, and leave open a later Weizenbaum version; the BUT delimiter, present in the 1965 code and in no version derived from the article, remains the clean test.

The vocabulary points the same way. Keystack is Weizenbaum's expository term, five times in the article's prose and absent from his source, and it is this program's central variable name. No function name in this program appears in the MAD-SLIP transcriptions, which on its own proves little, since a reimplementation in another language renames everything.

The program therefore cannot predate the text of the article: January 1966 if from print, autumn 1965 at the earliest if from the manuscript, received September 1965 and in circulation at MIT. With the 16 June 1966 line on I-UM0AG as the upper end, the window is narrow.

Descent. This is Bernie Cosell's DOCTOR, written at BBN in BBN LISP for the PDP-1, adapted for PDP-6 Lisp. Cosell's own paper tape of the program, "DOCTOR 10 JULY" (I-HJHZT), has the same matcher and reassembler under the same names, RECO1, TEST and TEST1 to TEST5, RECONSTRUCT, ADVANCE, MEMORY, SENTPRINT and MAKESENTENCE, with NEWKEY, LASTRESORT and the FLIPFLOP memory toggle; what differs is the input and driver layer (WORKER, READIN, READWORD, BREAKANALYZE, GOBBLE, SETKEYSTACK, INITIALIZE, CLEANUP), which a move between the two machines' Lisps would have to rewrite. The scripts on the tape are Cosell's script in two states: I-UM0AG, file SCRIP4 and headed "UPDATED TO 16 JUN 66", has the same seventy-two keywords in the same order as Cosell's paper tape "SCRIP 4.1 2 July 1966" (I-9G8JQ), and I-HDTE9 is an earlier state lacking seven of them. The adaptation therefore existed by 16 June 1966 and carries the earliest dated state of Cosell's script. The program then went on at the MIT AI Lab: collation with the 1978 ITS DOCTOR at I-E136U gives nineteen functions in common, ten of them token-identical, with DEFPROP and LAMBDA modernised to DEFUN; WORKER was rewritten, 1978 adds NEXTCH, and this copy carries debugging instrumentation (DISINI and DISPRINT inside TEST, an ARRAY FOO NIL 1700 buffer) and separate INITIALIZE and CLEANUP that 1978 folds into WORKER. This paragraph earlier stated that the function set is absent from Cosell's 1966 program; that came from a case-sensitive comparison with Cosell's lowercase file and was wrong (corrected 19 October 2026).

Dialect. Early PDP-6 Lisp, the MIT AI Lab Lisp that became Maclisp. Function definitions take the form (DEFPROP name (LAMBDA ...) EXPR); OBLIST is handled as a list, appended and rplaca'd through so that INITIALIZE and CLEANUP save and restore the object list, where Maclisp later used the OBARRAY hash array; ASCII is not assumed but built by hand from a PNAME property with (LSH X 29.), one 7-bit character left-justified in a 36-bit word; and 29. carries a decimal override against an octal default read base. The primitives assumed are READCH, READLIST, TERPRI, PRIN1, PRINC, FLATSIZE, CHRCT, INTERN, PUTPROP, RPLACA, GREATERP, ZEROP, ADD1, SUB1, LSH and PROG2. The debug code drives display hardware through DISINI, DISAD and DISLIST writing into (ARRAY FOO NIL 1700). I-E136U is the same program in Maclisp: DEFUN, DECLARE SPECIAL, SETSYNTAX, and ASCII called as a primitive.

Attribution. The program and its scripts are Cosell's (see Descent). Who adapted them for the PDP-6, and when they left BBN, is not recorded. The tape is labelled as Samson's, and no ELIZA file on it carries a name, while his compiler on the same tape is signed "P. SAMSON" in its TITLE line. Samson worked in this environment: dectape/samson/Subway/@.lisp in the same collection is a PDP-6 Lisp core image carrying the atom names SUBR, FSUBR, EXPR, PNAME, OBLIST, TERPRI, READCH, PRIN1, GREATERP, CHRCT, DEFPROP, DISINI and DISAD, the same Lisp and the same display package this program's debugging code uses, and his subway route work on the PDP-6 is documented for 1967. GROSS and GRUEN (gross, gruen) name nothing identifiable, and neither appears as a person in the Project MAC progress reports for 1965 to 1966 or 1966 to 1967. Weizenbaum is not a candidate: he worked in MAD-SLIP on CTSS. The German in the script is his own, inherited from the appendix, where XFREMD is the foreign-language catch-all; Cosell's encoding dropped XFREMD and hung the reply on DEUTSCH instead.

Already published elsewhere. All three files have been on elizagen since January 2024 in Other_Elizas/PDP6-ELIZA-1966-via-LarsBrinkhoff/, from Brinkhoff's email to Jeff Shrager of 16 January 2024, which notes that "some files on the same tape are dated 1965". The genealogy node is E03_SamsonXXLisp, whose XX leaves the date open, and the genealogy treats it as a separate program from Cosell's (node E01). As of 19 October 2026 the identification with Cosell's DOCTOR recorded here has not been reported to Jeff Shrager; David Berry will tell him.

items.creator: Cosell, Bernie (after Weizenbaum)
items.description:
A further developed Lisp DOCTOR script, read from GRUEN SCRIP4 in slot 17 of DECtape M46 (tape identifier P14) in Peter Samson's collection. Byte-identical to the copy in Lars Brinkhoff's its-vault repository, which is where it was read from.

It is SCRIP 4 of Bernie Cosell's DOCTOR script, from BBN, the state before his paper tape "SCRIP 4.1 2 July 1966" (I-9G8JQ): the two have the same seventy-two keywords in the same order, and their texts agree closely (similarity 0.918 with whitespace set aside).

325 lines against the 248 of I-HDTE9, and it departs from the CACM appendix where that one does not. It adds PRE rules to IF, ARE and YOU, a PUTPROP of NONE to LASTRESORT, SVENSKA to the foreign-language group, and keywords the appendix has no trace of: XXYYZZ for a monosyllabic user ("ARE YOU USING MONOSYLLABLES FOR SOME REASON"), BAG for "bite the bag", OH for "oh my" and "my oh my" routed through the sentinel ZZYYXX, and IS and WHERE. Keyword-sequence similarity against the appendix transcription at P-J415Q falls to 0.894.

The additions, all present in Cosell's SCRIP 4.1, are colloquial American English and add a language to the "I speak only English" joke.

items.creator: Cox, Irv (ELIZA); FREUD unattributed
items.description:

items.title: DOCTOR and ELIZA in Stanford LISP 1.6 for the PDP-10, DECUS 10-105, March 1970 (Lauck)
items.creator: Lauck, Tony (adapter)
items.dateBasis: The blurb DOCTOR.TXT is signed "/ TONY LAUCK 30-MAR-70". The BACKUP file attributes on the tape give write dates of 23 March 1970 (SPEC), 27 March 1970 (DOCPGM.LSP, DOCPGM.LAP, DOCTOR.RLS) and 30 March 1970 (DOCTOR.TXT, DUMP, ELIZA.RLS, DOCTOR.SAV, ELIZA.SAV). The stub 105.INF is dated 29 April 1975, the date of the library tape.
items.description:
The DECUS PDP-10 library package 10-105, "DOCTOR and ELIZA": the Lisp program DOCPGM.LSP, its compiled LAP code, two scripts (DOCTOR.RLS and ELIZA.RLS), a file of special declarations, dumping functions, two save files and Lauck's blurb. The blurb describes "SOURCES AND SAVE FILES OF DOCTOR AND ELIZA, ADAPTED FOR THE STANFORD A.I. LISP 1.6" and says the compiled version runs "UP TO SIX TIMES FASTER THAN PREVIOUS VERSIONS". The DECUS catalogue of February 1978 lists the author as "Anthony Lauk, et al" of Digital Equipment Corp., Maynard, and says "This version came from an old core image"; the original author is not named.

The program implements NEWKEY, a keystack ordered by priority against its top entry, and memory: a MEMR rule on MY stores reassembled sentences on NONE's MEM list, and ANALYZE alternates MEM and LASTRESORT through FLIPFLOP (initialised to 2 in the scripts), so a memory is offered on every second input with no keyword. Delimiters are the PUNCTUATION property (? ( , ! ) . : ;). It opens with a Dutch retelling of the anecdote of a vice president who took a DOCTOR program for a colleague at a remote terminal, prints a long English sample conversation, sets exercises on telling the computer's remarks from the user's, and ends with a BASIC listing on pp. 76-79. REM lines 20-40 read "-ELIZA- IN EEN BEWERKING VAN:" and "-GUUS WISELIUS-" ("in an adaptation by Guus Wiselius").

The program uses SUBSTR(string,start,length) in place of MID$, has Dutch prompts ("MIJN DENKTIJD IS TOT +/- 30 SECONDEN") and a test switch (Q1) that prints intermediate values; the dialogue is in English. The dream keyword and its replies are replaced by sex ("DO YOU LIKE FUCKING?", "WHAT DO YOU FEEL WHILE MAKING LOVE?"). Keywords are scanned in list order and the first found wins; no clause splitting, no NEWKEY, no memory. Features were read from the OCR text and page images; the apology spelling was not settled from the OCR.

items.description:
An English ELIZA for the ZX Spectrum, credited to M. de Vries in the archive.org title, which marks the author as Dutch ("NL"). It opens with "Hi,I'm Eliza,whats your problem?", strips punctuation and lower-cases the input, answers an empty line with "Well,say something!!!" and "shut up" with "There is no need to be rude!!" before stopping. items.description:
ELISA, a German ELIZA that speaks its replies, typed into an Amstrad CPC 464 by Michael Wessel in Hamburg c. 1985 from the German edition of Ahl's BASIC Computer Games ("BASIC-Computer-Spiele", Sybex, Düsseldorf, 1982; translator Wolfgang J. The keyword search, conjugation and reply rotation are those of the Creative Computing program, with the keywords translated ("KANNST DU", "KANN ICH", "DU BIST" ... "COMPUTER", "KEIN SCHLUESSELWORT" for NOKEYFOUND). Line 530, the conjugation swap, omits "+r$", so a matched word is deleted instead of being replaced; the bytes on both disks agree. LS195.dsk (LambdaSpeak 1.95) holds DEMO01.BAS, ELISA-DK.BAS (12,775 bytes), ELIZA.BAS (35,329 bytes) and SPRACHE.BAS (5,340 bytes, the standalone German speech driver). LS300.dsk (LambdaSpeak 3) holds 27 files, among them ELISA-DK.BAS and ELISASPO.BAS (identical apart from line 5, which selects the DK'tronics emulation, &EC, or the SPO256 native mode, &E1) and SPO-GERM.BAS; full directories are held as listings.

items.description:
Paul Gerard's ELIZA for the Amstrad CPC 464, a type-in published in two parts in the Australian magazine The Amstrad User in May and June 1986. The opening REM lines say the original "was programmed in LISP by Joseph Weizenbaum" and that BASIC versions by Jeff Shrager, Steve North and Tim Hartnell have appeared. A loader shows "Dr. ELIZA's waiting room" (Time magazines from 1972, a 1936 children's encyclopaedia) and runs ELIZA2, which asks for the user's name, confirms it, and uses it in later replies.

ELIZA2 holds 190 keywords or phrases, each with four replies chosen at random (the previous reply number is not repeated), 37 conjugation pairs, 24 insults, 24 swear words, 24 compliments, 25 replies for no keyword and five farewell words. Keys are scanned in list order and the first match wins. Input is cleaned of control characters and punctuation; at a comma, colon, semicolon, bracket or hyphen the program keeps only the part of the sentence on one side of it. Features read from the listing: no BUT delimiter, no NEWKEY, no keystack, no MEMORY, no XFREMD, no APOLIGIZE ("Don't apologise, please !"). The NVG note says swear words censored in the magazine listing were kept as printed.

items.title: ELIZA in SWTPC 8K BASIC 2.0 for the SWTPC 6800, letter in Creative Computing, March-April 1978 (Stock)
items.creator: Stock, William
items.dateBasis: Issue date of Creative Computing vol. 4 no. 2, March-April 1978 (archive.org metadata and file name). The port was running by the time the letter was written.
items.description:
A reader's letter headed "ELIZA" from William Stock of Cincinnati, replying to Steve North's July-August 1977 article. North had remarked on running the program on a Southwest 6800, and Stock writes: "With some minor restrictions and coding changes, I now have Eliza up and running." Response time averaged 15 seconds; replies and input had to be cut to 32 characters. He proposes finding the spaces once and testing keywords only at word starts, skipping the search for NOKEYFOUND, and conjugating only when the reply ends in an asterisk.

Steve North's reply follows. He notes that SWTPC 8K BASIC first allowed strings of only 16 characters and that version 2.0, which Stock used, allows 32; that NOKEYFOUND is a dummy kept "mainly for documentation purposes", with keyword 36 set at line 370 when nothing matches; and that he aimed at a program that was "fairly straightforward and understandable".

The port itself is not held; no listing was printed. Its features are unknown beyond the changes the letter describes.

Source: archive.org item creativecomputing-1978-03, page 12 of the issue PDF (printed p. 8), whose md5 and sha1 matched the item metadata before cutting.

items.description:
The script and program appendices of Shapiro and Kwasny, "Interactive Consulting via Natural Language", Indiana University Computer Science Department Technical Report 12, June 1974: Appendix I, "Keywords used for ELIZA Helper"; Appendix II, "Script for ELIZA Helper"; and Appendix III, "Cal SNOBOL Version of ELIZA", a full program listing. Chapter 7 of John Krutch's book, published by Howard W. Sams & Co., Indianapolis, explains Weizenbaum's ELIZA, walks through each routine of a BASIC DOCTOR, and prints the full listing headed "DOCTOR, Vers. 2.1". items.description:
The Software Toolworks' ELIZA, written by Walt Bilofsky, is an interpreter for Weizenbaum's script language that reads rule lists from a script file. This IBM PC disk holds the interpreter ELIZA.COM, with the banner "ELIZA 1.0 (10/8/82)", and two scripts: ODOCTOR.SCR, "the original DOCTOR script", and DOCTOR.SCR, "the current DOCTOR script", in the manual's words. The manual calls the program "a faithful recreation of Dr. Weizenbaum's original script interpreter".

The manual describes keyword priorities with a keystack (a keyword of higher priority "is placed on top of the stack. Otherwise, it is placed on the bottom"), NEWKEY, PRE, DLIST and NONE, and MEMORY rules recalled "When five responses have passed" since the last MEMORY use. Input is split into sentences at "any punctuation such as period, comma, dash"; BUT appears in the scripts only inside replies. ODOCTOR.SCR keeps the XFREMD rule ("(DEUTSCH (=XFREMD))" and the reply "I AM SORRY, I SPEAK ONLY ENGLISH"); DOCTOR.SCR removes it, splits NONE replies by input length and adds MEMORY patterns. Both spell "APOLOGIZE" correctly. ELIZA.COM also contains the string "(c) J Gillogly", probably a shared Toolworks code credit (inferred).

The user manual, from the vgmuseum "firstera" collection, is held privately: Bilofsky’s licence of 2025 covers his ELIZA files, and the manual is not among them. It is undated beyond its title page and may have been written for the 1981 CP/M and HDOS release.

items.title: ELIZA version 3.0 in Applesoft BASIC for the Apple II, 1981 (Grumette; Applesoft translation by Kessler)
items.creator: Grumette, Steve; Kessler, Will (Applesoft translation)
items.dateBasis: Screen text at line 32: "COPYRIGHT (C) 1981 BY STEVE GRUMETTE". The disk images are undated.
items.description:
Steve Grumette's ELIZA 3.0, "TRANSLATED TO APPLESOFT BY WILL KESSLER", opens with "HOW DO YOU DO.  PLEASE TELL ME YOUR PROBLEM.". It follows the CACM DOCTOR script: substitutions, keywords including DEUTSCH, ESPANOL, FRANCAIS, ITALIANO, REMEMBER and EVERYBODY, and replies such as "I'VE TOLD YOU THAT APOLOGIES ARE NOT REQUIRED.". A machine-language routine does the string searches.

Input is broken into clauses at punctuation and each clause is searched in turn. Of 44 keywords, any of the first 20 found is taken at once in list order; otherwise the leftmost of the rest wins, a two-tier priority without a keystack. A keyword routine that finds no matching pattern returns 0 and the scan goes on to the next keyword (line 560), which works like NEWKEY though the name is not used. Clauses after "YOUR" are queued in M$() and, on a clause with no keyword, the oldest is recalled with one of four memory replies ("BUT YOUR" among them) when the input counter NE exceeds 5 (line 6000); the counter is reset at each recall. The foreign-language keywords give "I AM SORRY, I SPEAK ONLY ENGLISH.". The program also keeps a conversation buffer with DISPLAY, SAVE, CLEAR and RESTART commands.

The Eliza_3.0 disk holds four conversation buffers saved by users (ALIEN, KOOK, YES, GFHHGJJF), undated; they are held as text in an alternate zip with the shipped SAMPLE.TXT.

items.description:
ELIZA version 3.11, "Lattice C version of ELIZA defined by Dr.Wizenbaum", printed as section 5-3-1 of Yasui Tsutomu's book on the NEC PC-9801 V series, PC-Techknow 98V (1986). The section introduces ELIZA as a classic of natural language processing research, notes that the original was written in "MAD-Slip" and that the program is also called DOCTOR, and gives a flowchart, the source eliza.c, the reply file ELIZA.TXT (read with fseek, its lines padded to 64 bytes by a program FORM64.C printed in the book's appendix and not held), the compile log (Lattice MS-DOS C Compiler 3.00, Microsoft linker 3.00) and a short sample run.

The program has 43 keyword patterns written with wildcards *0 (any number of words) and *1 (one word), from "*0 do I remember *0" and "*0 you remember *0" to "*0 because *0" and "*0 are *0"; the first matching pattern in list order is used and replies rotate per keyword (tables replydata and variate). A synonym routine (noder) maps words to class heads, a device comparable to the DLIST classes of the CACM script. items.title: Sussex Mini ELIZA in POP-11, 1978, file as revised to 1986 (Sloman after Hardy)
items.creator: Sloman, Aaron; Hardy, Steve
items.dateBasis: Revision history at the end of the held file: "Aaron Sloman, May 17 1978 - modified and expanded. Based on simple version by S.Hardy", "A.Sloman Oct 1981 - modified for VAXPOP", "Aaron Sloman, Sep 28 1986 fixed author, tabified", then "John Gibson, Jul 7 1995 Made it compile under 14.53"; header "Copyright University of Sussex 1995". The program text is the 1986 state with a 1995 compile fix. A comment on the procedure gtrl reads "added 19 sept 1979". The alternates carry the revision dates 15 January 2005, 18 July 2009 and 19 October 2011; TEACH ELIZA is headed "Steve Hardy, October 1981" and TEACH ELIZA2 "Steven Hardy, November 1981".
items.description:
The Sussex Mini ELIZA, the conversation program of the Sussex POP-11 teaching system, held in the state the file had reached by 28 September 1986. Aaron Sloman expanded it on 17 May 1978 from a simple version by Steve Hardy, added an interactive NEWRULE command on 19 September 1979 (the user types NEWRULE and composes a rule in dialogue), and adapted it for VAX POP in October 1981; John Gibson made it compile under Poplog 14.53 in July 1995. The program opens with "Good day what is your problem" and its jokes belong to the period ("Have you talked to Margaret Thatcher about that?").

Each input is lower-cased, leading words such as "well", "but" and "however" are dropped, and the person of the sentence is changed; the list of rule procedures is then shuffled and tried in turn until one leaves a reply. A rule named "earlier" fires with probability 12 in 100 once more than ten inputs have passed, and prefixes a stored earlier sentence with "earlier you said", "I recall your saying" or "what did you mean by saying". MEMORY is marked true for this stored-sentence device; it has no fixed period and is unrelated in code to Weizenbaum's MEMORY. A rule "verynasty", added in 1981, writes new rules at run time with popval. There is no BUT delimiter, no NEWKEY, no keystack and no XFREMD; features were read from the held 1986-state source.

Alternates: the Birmingham states of 2005, 2009 and 2011 (the 2011 file is about three and a half times the size of the 1986 file; two editor backups of the 2011 file, elizaprog.p- and elizaprog.p--, were seen and left out), and Hardy's teaching files TEACH ELIZA and TEACH ELIZA2 of October and November 1981. No 1978 or 1981 copy of the program is known; those states survive only as revision notes. Sloman's TEACH RESPOND (revised 20 October 1987) and TEACH MINI.ELIZA (October 1997) were seen on the same server and not held.

Source: the Poplog file tree at poplog.fricas.org (University of Birmingham mirror), "discarded" area for the 1986 state and packages/teaching for the later states and TEACH files; server dates 14 September 2024. No checksums are published.

items.title: Colby, Watt and Gilbert's psychotherapy program in SUBALGOL, IBM 7090 via PDP-1, April 1965: the 1966 paper
items.creator: Colby, Kenneth Mark; Watt, James B.; Gilbert, John P.
items.dateBasis: The paper states "At the time of writing (April, 1965) the program had about 500 keys". Published in The Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease 142(2), 1966 ("Vol. 142, No. 2", copyright 1966, on the first page).
items.description:
The only evidence held for the program: Colby, Watt and Gilbert's paper "A Computer Method of Psychotherapy: Preliminary Communication". The program itself is not held, and no copy is known. A person at a teletype connected to a PDP-1, which passed the text to the Stanford IBM 7090, typed statements in ordinary English and received replies. The paper says "Our program is coded in SUBALGOL" and that the PDP-1 program was written by Michael Levitt; in April 1965 it had "about 500 keys".

As the paper describes it, keys run from single words to phrases of up to four words, replies depend on the stage of the session, pronouns are changed in reflected statements, and topics are tracked for later use. It cites Weizenbaum's program as the first of the kind, run on MIT's MAC time-sharing system.

Source: Stanford Digital Repository, Edward A. Feigenbaum papers (SC0340, accession 1986-052, box 52, folder 17), item hk334rq4790. The PDF and its OCR text were checked against the sha1 and md5 digests in the repository's public metadata.

items.dateBasis: ERIC resume of ED052482: "PUB DATE Jan 70"; title page "Project Report No. 29".
items.description:
The only evidence held for GLURP: the body and the GLURP appendices of the ISVD report describing it. The processor itself is not held; the report contains no assembler listing. GLURP is described as "a mid-point version" of the script-writing language intended for ISVD. Its scripts mix TRAC functions with "the non-TRAC "DECOMP" statement which is actually a blend of ELIZA and TRAC": DECOMP rules use ELIZA-style patterns with 0 as a wildcard and named rule lists (POS, NEG and others), and transfer to a numbered step on a match.

The report covers GLURP as it then existed, its interface to the RCA BTSS time-sharing system and adaptation to other BAL-oriented machines, and its faults. Appendix E is the MINORCA specification by Dorothy Swithenbank and Arnold Smith, ISVD's earlier author language.
